title: Eliminating Data Serialization Overhead with Apache Arrow
author: Aniket Abhishek Soni
summary: You ship the job. It passes CI. Then, during the first production run, you watch your memory usage spike and your CPU sit at 100% while the task manager reports minimal actual data throughput. The bottleneck isn't your algorithm; it is the silent, invisible tax of serialization. Every time you move data between systems—say, from a Python pandas DataFrame to a PySpark worker or from an in-memory database to an Apache Arrow-aware API—you are likely triggering a "copy-and-convert" cycle. Most systems store data in formats optimized for their own internal logic, usually row-based (like standard Python lists of dictionaries). To talk to another system, they must walk through the entire structure, translate it into a byte stream, send it over the wire or local memory, and then force the receiving system to re-parse that stream into its own internal memory layout. This is where Apache Arrow changes the calculus. Instead of forcing systems to translate data, Arrow provides a standardized, language-agnostic columnar memory format that stays consistent across the entire stack. How it actually works At its core, Apache Arrow (as defined in the Apache Arrow specification ) is a specification for how data should be laid out in memory to be processed by CPUs as efficiently as possible. Consider a hypothetical dataset of user transactions with two columns: user_id (integer) and amount (float). In a traditional row-based approach, you store these as [user_id, amount], [user_id, amount] . If you only need to calculate the average of amount , the CPU has to fetch the entire row, parse the user_id , skip it, and extract the amount . You are loading unnecessary bytes into your CPU cache. Arrow uses a columnar layout. In memory, it stores all user_id values in one contiguous block and all amount values in another. Because the data is contiguous, modern CPUs can use SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) instructions to perform operations on multiple values in a single clock cycle. To see this in action, imagine you are using pyarrow to move data between a Parquet file and a memory-mapped buffer. Because Parquet uses the same columnar structure as Arrow, the "loading" process becomes a zero-copy operation. You aren't parsing; you are simply mapping the file bytes directly into your process's memory space. import pyarrow.parquet as pq import pyarrow as pa # Hypothetical scenario: Loading a 10GB Parquet file # By using memory mapping, we avoid reading the whole file into RAM table = pq . read_table ( ' transactions.parquet ' , memory_map = True ) # Because this is already in Arrow format, we can pass this table # to other libraries (like Polars or DuckDB) without copying the underlying memory. print ( table . schema ) The key here is the memory_map=True flag. When you do this, the operating system maps the file on disk into the virtual address space of your process. The CPU fetches the data only when the code explicitly touches the memory pages. There is no intermediate transformation layer. Photo by Shubham Dhage on Unsplash Design choices and tradeoffs While Arrow is an engineering marvel, it is not a "free lunch." The primary design choice in Arrow is the trade-off between CPU efficiency and memory footprint . Because Arrow is optimized for fast access, it often uses "padding" and fixed-width buffers to ensure that data elements are aligned with CPU cache lines. In a row-based system, a compressed string might be tiny because you are squeezing it into a compact format. In Arrow, that same string might be stored with additional metadata or null-bitmaps to ensure the next column starts at a clean memory address. This leads to what engineers call "memory inflation." A dataset that occupies 1GB on disk in a heavily compressed format might easily balloon to 2GB or 3GB when loaded into Arrow format in memory. If your cluster nodes have tight memory limits, switching to an Arrow-based workflow can lead to OutOfMemory errors that were not present when using row-based iterators. Another tradeoff is API complexity . While Arrow provides a stable, high-performance foundation, the library surface area (especially in pyarrow or arrow-cpp ) is massive. You are managing memory buffers, null bitmaps, and schema definitions at a low level. If you are building a wrapper, you are responsible for ensuring that the buffers remain valid for the lifetime of the application—if the underlying file or buffer is closed, you will trigger a segmentation fault. Photo by Laura Ockel on Unsplash When to reach for it (and when not to) You should reach for Arrow when you are performing high-frequency data movement between analytical engines. If you are using modern tools like DuckDB , Polars , or Apache Spark (which uses Arrow for its PySpark to Pandas conversion via toPandas() ), Arrow is doing the heavy lifting behind the scenes. Use it explicitly when: You are building custom connectors or data loaders where you control the memory lifecycle. You are passing large chunks of data between different Python processes or libraries where serialization (like pickle or json ) is becoming a latency bottleneck. You need to perform complex analytical queries on data that is too large to fit in memory but small enough to be memory-mapped. Do not reach for Arrow if: Your application is primarily doing row-based lookups (e.g., fetching a single user record by ID from a key-value store). The overhead of managing the Arrow schema and memory buffers will outweigh the benefits of columnar access. You are working with small datasets (a few megabytes). The cost of setting up the Arrow memory buffers will be higher than just using a native Python list or dictionary. You are constrained by extremely low-memory environments, such as small Lambda functions or edge containers, where the memory inflation caused by Arrow padding could cause your process to be killed by the OOM killer. Conclusion Apache Arrow is the "glue" of the modern data stack. By standardizing the format of data in memory, it eliminates the need for expensive serialization, turning what used to be a compute-bound conversion task into a simple memory pointer update. As an engineer, your job is to identify where these conversion bottlenecks exist. Look for high-latency points where data is being moved between libraries or processes. If you find your system spending more time "preparing" data than "processing" it, you are likely paying a serialization tax that Arrow was designed to eliminate. title: 48-Hour Field Notes: Same Prompt, Two JSON Shapes, and a Validator That Passed Both
author: Taylor Wang
summary: Six hundred markdown files landed in an inbox folder, and my only job was to turn them into a one-page morning report. The plan looked trivial: send each file to a model, get back four fields, append a line of JSONL, render a table. I gave myself forty-eight hours to make that loop boring, so like an idiot I built the happy path first. The happy path held for about six hours. The full run exited 0, the report rendered, and nobody on the receiving end noticed that one column had quietly stopped meaning anything. These are the field notes: what I tried, where it broke, and the small harness I would keep for next time. The constraints I actually had Before the timeline makes sense, here is the shape of the problem. Roughly 600 small text files per night, growing by maybe 5% a week. Four output fields per file: category , severity , needs_human , summary . A morning report that a human reads, so a wrong column is worse than a missing row. No budget, which meant a free tier and a free machine, and no assumption of either staying stable. That last one is the constraint people skip, and it produced every bug below. If your model access can change shape between Tuesday and Wednesday, then your real interface is not the API — it is the contract you wrote down and test. Hour 0–6: the validator that agreed with everything I wrote the extraction call, a parser, and a validator, and all three passed on the first twenty files. The validator was a dataclass with type annotations checked by isinstance , which felt rigorous and was mostly theater. # validate_v0.py -- the version that lied to me FIELDS = { " category " : str , " severity " : str , " needs_human " : bool , " summary " : str } def validate_v0 ( payload : dict ) -> list [ str ]: errors = [] for key , expected in FIELDS . items (): if key not in payload : errors . append ( f " missing { key } " ) elif not isinstance ( payload [ key ], expected ): errors . append ( f " { key } is { type ( payload [ key ]). __name__ } " ) return errors Do you see what is missing? Nothing checks the values . severity: str accepts "high" and "P1" and "HIGH " with a trailing space, and all three pass the same test. My validator was answering "is this a string" when the report needed "is this one of three levels". Hour 6–18: moving to the free server and 19 quiet repairs I moved the batch onto MonkeyCode's free server option, which is where the overnight run was supposed to live, and used its free model access for the extraction step. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. I treat both of those as conveniences rather than guarantees, which is why nothing below hardcodes a model name, a quota, or a machine size. The only thing I actually rely on is that a call returns text, and that text usually contains a JSON object. Nineteen of six hundred responses failed to parse, so I added a repair loop with a budget of one extra call. Nineteen became zero, the job exited 0, and I went to bed feeling clever. That feeling cost me a morning. def extract_json ( text : str ) -> dict : start , end = text . find ( " { " ), text . rfind ( " } " ) if start == - 1 or end <= start : raise ValueError ( " no JSON object found in model output " ) return json . loads ( text [ start : end + 1 ]) Hour 18–30: the report that looked fine and was not The morning report rendered beautifully and the severity column was garbage. Two thirds of the rows said high , medium , or low , and the rest said P1 , Sev-2 , and one memorable critical! . No exception fired, no row was dropped, and the chart at the top just looked like a bad week. This is the failure mode I keep relearning: a schema that only checks structure will happily certify a semantic regression . The model had not broken. My contract had never specified the value domain, so the model was free to answer the question it thought I asked. What would you have checked at hour 18? I checked row counts, because row counts are the thing that goes wrong in demos. Row count was perfect. Hour 30–42: the artifact I should have written first I spent the next twelve hours building a shape checker, and it is the only part of this project I would keep. The idea is simple: fingerprint the structure of every response, pin the domain of every enumerated field, and make any deviation a non-zero exit code. 1. Fingerprint the shape, not the text # fingerprint.py from __future__ import annotations import hashlib import json from typing import Any def type_name ( value : Any ) -> str : if value is None : return " null " if isinstance ( value , bool ): # before int: bool subclasses int return " bool " if isinstance ( value , int ): return " int " if isinstance ( value , float ): return " float " if isinstance ( value , str ): return " str " if isinstance ( value , list ): return " list " if isinstance ( value , dict ): return " dict " return type ( value ). __name__ def shape_of ( obj : Any , prefix : str = "" ) -> dict [ str , str ]: """ Map every JSON path in a payload to a type name. """ out : dict [ str , str ] = {} if isinstance ( obj , dict ): for key in sorted ( obj ): path = f " { prefix } . { key } " if prefix else key out [ path ] = type_name ( obj [ key ]) out . update ( shape_of ( obj [ key ], path )) elif isinstance ( obj , list ): if not obj : out [ f " { prefix } [] " ] = " empty " else : out [ f " { prefix } [] " ] = type_name ( obj [ 0 ]) out . update ( shape_of ( obj [ 0 ], f " { prefix } [] " )) return out def fingerprint ( payload : dict ) -> str : blob = json . dumps ( sorted ( shape_of ( payload ). items ()), separators = ( " , " , " : " )) return hashlib . sha256 ( blob . encode ()). hexdigest () Note the bool -before- int ordering, because isinstance(True, int) is True and that single line has burned me before. Note also that the fingerprint hashes key paths and type names only, so a reworded summary does not trip the alarm while a nested object where a string used to be does. 2. Pin the value domains Structure alone would not have caught the P1 problem, so the contract also declares allowed values and fails on anything outside them. # contract.py from __future__ import annotations from dataclasses import dataclass , field from fingerprint import shape_of EXPECTED_SHAPE = { " category " : " str " , " severity " : " str " , " needs_human " : " bool " , " summary " : " str " , } ALLOWED_VALUES = { " category " : { " billing " , " bug " , " account " , " other " }, " severity " : { " low " , " medium " , " high " }, } @dataclass class Report : missing : list [ str ] = field ( default_factory = list ) unexpected : list [ str ] = field ( default_factory = list ) retyped : list [ str ] = field ( default_factory = list ) out_of_domain : list [ str ] = field ( default_factory = list ) @property def ok ( self ) -> bool : return not ( self . missing or self . unexpected or self . retyped or self . out_of_domain ) def render ( self ) -> str : lines = [] if self . missing : lines . append ( f " missing: { self . missing } " ) if self . unexpected : lines . append ( f " unexpected: { self . unexpected } " ) if self . retyped : lines . append ( f " retyped: { self . retyped } " ) if self . out_of_domain : lines . append ( f " out of domain: { self . out_of_domain } " ) return " \n " . join ( lines ) or " ok " def check ( payload : dict ) -> Report : report = Report () shape = shape_of ( payload ) for path , expected in EXPECTED_SHAPE . items (): actual = shape . get ( path ) if actual is None : report . missing . append ( path ) elif actual != expected : report . retyped . append ( f " { path } : { actual } != { expected } " ) for path in shape : if path not in EXPECTED_SHAPE : report . unexpected . append ( path ) for path , allowed in ALLOWED_VALUES . items (): value = payload . get ( path ) if isinstance ( value , str ) and value . strip () not in allowed : report . out_of_domain . append ( f " { path } = { value !r} " ) return report Yes, this contract is a flat dictionary, and yes, that is deliberate — the moment I added nesting I needed a second fingerprint for each child shape. 3. Replay saved responses instead of calling the model The part that saved the most time was writing every raw response to disk with a content hash, then testing the validator against those files. Validation bugs are cheap to fix offline and expensive to find at 3 a.m. mkdir -p fixtures/raw out python run_batch.py \ --inbox inbox/ \ --out out/report.jsonl \ --raw fixtures/raw \ --repair-budget 1 # what actually landed in the report? jq -r '.severity' out/report.jsonl | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn # tests/test_contract_replay.py import pathlib import pytest from contract import check from run_batch import extract_json RAW = sorted ( pathlib . Path ( " fixtures/raw " ). glob ( " *.txt " )) @pytest.mark.parametrize ( " path " , RAW , ids = [ p . name for p in RAW ]) def test_saved_response_matches_contract ( path ): payload = extract_json ( path . read_text ()) report = check ( payload ) assert report . ok , f " { path . name } \n { report . render () } " Forty saved responses run in under a second and cost nothing, which means I can change the contract and immediately see which historical responses I would now reject. That is a much better feedback loop than re-running the batch and squinting at a table. 4. Make drift a non-zero exit code # run_batch.py (core loop, trimmed) import hashlib import pathlib import sys from contract import check from fingerprint import fingerprint FAIL_RATIO = 0.02 def handle ( path : pathlib . Path , call_model , raw_dir : pathlib . Path , repair_budget : int ) -> dict : prompt = build_prompt ( path . read_text ()) payload = None text = "" for attempt in range ( repair_budget + 1 ): text = call_model ( prompt if attempt == 0 else repair_prompt ( prompt , text )) digest = hashlib . sha256 ( text . encode ()). hexdigest ()[: 12 ] ( raw_dir / f " { path . stem } - { digest } .txt " ). write_text ( text ) try : payload = extract_json ( text ) break except ValueError : continue if payload is None : raise ValueError ( f " no parseable JSON for { path . name } " ) return { " source " : path . name , " fingerprint " : fingerprint ( payload ), ** payload } results = [ handle ( p , call_model , raw_dir , args . repair_budget ) for p in inbox ] drift = [ r for r in results if not check ( r ). ok ] if drift : sys . exit ( 2 ) if repairs / max ( len ( results ), 1 ) > FAIL_RATIO : sys . exit ( 3 ) Exit code 2 is intentionally separate from 3, because drift means "the world changed" and a high repair rate means "the model is struggling" — different humans should be woken up for those. Hour 42–48: three live runs and the second drift On the second live run, needs_human came back as the string "false" on four rows. Under my old validator that would have been a truthy string that marked everything as needing a human. Under the new contract it was a retyped path, exit code 2, and a one-line message on the terminal. Three runs later I had a golden set of forty responses, a contract that fails loudly, and a repair budget I could tune without lying to myself about failure rates. Nothing about that is clever, and that is exactly the point. Decision table: repair, retry, or fail closed This is the table I wish I had written on hour one. Symptom Signal Action Response has no JSON object parse error one repair call, then fail the row JSON parses, key missing contract missing fail closed, do not backfill a default JSON parses, extra key appears contract unexpected fail closed, log the raw hash Value outside the domain contract out_of_domain fail closed, never map to "other" silently Type changed contract retyped fail closed, this is drift not noise Repair rate above 2% run summary alert, quarantine the run's output The pattern is boring on purpose: repair is only for unparseable text, and everything semantic fails closed. Every time I let a validator "fix" a value, I created a bug that took longer to find than the original failure did. What I would repeat, and what I would throw away Repeat: writing the contract before the prompt, saving raw responses with hashes, replaying fixtures offline, and splitting exit codes by failure class. Throw away: the repair-on-any-error loop, the str -typed enums, and the row-count smoke test that told me nothing. I would also keep the free tier for what it is good at — a nightly batch at this size, on a machine I do not have to own. It is not a plan for ten times the volume, and I have not tested what happens then. Limitations and who should skip this Three honest limits. A fingerprint detects change, not correctness. If the model returns the wrong category with the right shape, this harness passes it. The domains are hand-written. {"billing", "bug", "account", "other"} came from reading fifty files, so it is a guess with a changelog. The fixtures are a snapshot. Forty saved responses are evidence about those forty responses, not a distribution. Skip this if you read every output yourself, or if your provider offers a strict schema mode you can enforce at generation time — that is a stronger guarantee than a post-hoc checker. Skip it too if the output reaches customers without a human seeing it first, because a contract test is not a review process. If you only take one thing: write down the shape and the allowed values before you write the prompt, then make drift fail the build. Your future self gets to sleep through the night, and that is worth twelve hours of anyone's weekend.

title: Historical tennis closing odds for past tournaments, in Python
author: Aurelix Solutions
summary: A tennis model or a betting system is only as good as the backtest behind it, and a backtest needs the market's closing prices for the matches you test on. Daily feeds give you that from now on; for last year's Wimbledon or the 2023 Paris Masters you need the archive. BetExplorer keeps one public results page per tournament season with the closing odds of every match, and each match page lists the closing price of every bookmaker it tracked. This post turns those pages into rows in Python, checks how often the closing favourite won, and notes what the archive does and doesn't contain. Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the Tennis Odds Scraper , which reads these pages in its History mode. It's a paid tool (prices below). Check the Store page before you buy: prices change. Finding a season On betexplorer.com, go to Tennis, pick the tour (ATP Singles, WTA Singles, Challenger...), the tournament and Results, then choose the year. Past seasons have their own path: /tennis/atp-singles/paris-2023/results/ /tennis/wta-singles/wimbledon-2023/results/ Use the path, not a ?year= link: BetExplorer's robots.txt asks bots not to fetch those query URLs, so the tool reads seasons by path only (a ?year=2023 link you paste is rewritten to the -2023 path). Every match of a season with closing odds pip install apify-client import os from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ " APIFY_TOKEN " ]) run = client . actor ( " aurelix/tennis-odds-scraper " ). call ( run_input = { " mode " : " history " , " seasons " : [ " /tennis/atp-singles/paris-2023/results/ " , " /tennis/wta-singles/wimbledon-2023/results/ " , ], " bookmakerOdds " : True , " maxResults " : 500 , } ) rows = list ( client . dataset ( run [ " defaultDatasetId " ]). iterate_items ()) print ( len ( rows ), " matches " ) Each row is one match: tournament ("Paris 2023"), round ("Final", "Semi-finals", "1/8-finals"...), date , category , match_type . player1 / player2 as BetExplorer lists them ("Djokovic N."), and with match pages on player1_full_name , player1_url , score ( 6-4 6-3 ) and set_scores . status : finished, retired, walkover or canceled; winner , winner_name , sets_p1 / sets_p2 . odds_p1 / odds_p2 : BetExplorer's average closing odds; implied_prob_p1 / p2 with the margin removed and the overround . bookmaker_odds : each listed bookmaker's closing price and the time it was set; closing_avg_* and closing_best_* across them. In the 2023 Paris final, for example, BetExplorer's average closing odds were 1.33 for Djokovic and 3.34 for Dimitrov, with 12 bookmakers listed; Djokovic won 6-4 6-3. How often did the closing favourite win? done = [ r for r in rows if r [ " status " ] in ( " finished " , " retired " ) and r [ " odds_p1 " ] and r [ " odds_p2 " ]] fav = sum (( r [ " odds_p1 " ] < r [ " odds_p2 " ]) == ( r [ " winner " ] == " player1 " ) for r in done ) print ( f " { fav } of { len ( done ) } matches ( { fav / len ( done ) : . 0 % } ) went to the closing favourite " ) On those two seasons it was 72% each: 38 of 53 priced matches in Paris 2023 and 88 of 123 at Wimbledon 2023 (women's singles). That is the base rate any model has to beat, and the implied probabilities tell you how much the market already knew. For a calibration check, bucket implied_prob_p1 and compare it with how often player 1 actually won in each bucket; with a few seasons of Grand Slams and Masters you have thousands of matches. Several seasons into one table import csv with open ( " closing_odds.csv " , " w " , newline = "" , encoding = " utf-8 " ) as f : w = csv . writer ( f ) w . writerow ([ " tournament " , " round " , " date " , " player1 " , " player2 " , " winner " , " odds_p1 " , " odds_p2 " , " best_p1 " , " best_p2 " , " bookmakers " ]) for r in rows : w . writerow ([ r [ " tournament " ], r [ " round " ], r [ " date " ], r [ " player1 " ], r [ " player2 " ], r [ " winner_name " ], r [ " odds_p1 " ], r [ " odds_p2 " ], r [ " closing_best_p1 " ], r [ " closing_best_p2 " ], r [ " bookmakers_count " ]]) match_id ( bx-l81rCxw4 ) is BetExplorer's own match code, so a second run of the same season returns the same IDs; with incremental on it returns nothing new and charges nothing for matches. What the archive does not have Opening odds. The match pages show each bookmaker's closing price; the opening price and the moves in between are not in the archive pages this mode reads. For matches from now on, the tool's Results mode reads TennisExplorer, which has opening and closing per bookmaker. Surface and rankings. Not on these pages; join them from the tournament's surface and a ranking history if your model needs them. Names as listed. List names are "Surname I."; full names come from match pages (on by default). Times. The time each closing price was set is read as the site's Prague time and converted to UTC. Cost $3.00 per 1,000 matches ($2.50 on paid plans), per-bookmaker closing odds included, plus a $0.005 start fee per run. A Grand Slam draw is about 127 matches, so a season costs about $0.39 on the free plan; Apify's free plan includes $5 of credit a month. Matches outside your filters, beyond maxResults or already returned in only-new mode are not charged. That is less than the dedicated BetExplorer tools on the Apify Store charge, and bookmaker odds cost nothing extra. title: Docs That Expire With the Code: Binding Every Generated Claim to a Source Digest
author: Avery Lin
summary: A generated documentation line is only as trustworthy as its provenance, and fluent prose carries no provenance at all. The workflow below forces every model-written line to cite a concrete code artifact together with that artifact's digest at draft time. When the code moves, the digest changes, the citation goes stale, and the build fails before any reviewer spends attention on the page. This is a generation-time gate rather than a review-time ceremony, and it needs two standard-library scripts and one decision table. Why Review Is the Wrong Place to Catch Drift A signoff gate answers a policy question about who approved a sentence, and it says nothing about whether the sentence is still true. Reviewers rarely reopen the source file a paragraph describes, so stale prose passes approval and then rots quietly for months. Digests invert the incentive: the doc has to prove freshness mechanically, and the human reviews only the judgement calls that code cannot settle. You do not need an LLM provider to adopt this, but if you already draft with one, the citation rules below are cheap to add. Step 1 — Build a Claim-Addressable Evidence Index The index converts your repository into a list of addressable facts, each with a stable id and a short content digest. Public function and class signatures, environment variable lookups, and CLI flags give you most of what a reference page actually asserts. Save this as evidence_index.py and note that ast.unparse requires Python 3.9 or newer. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ Build a claim-addressable evidence index from a Python repo. """ import ast , hashlib , json , pathlib , re , sys ENV_RE = re . compile ( r """ os\.(?:environ\.get|getenv)\(\s*[ "' ]([A-Z][A-Z0-9_]+)[ "' ] """ ) CLI_RE = re . compile ( r """ add_argument\(\s*[ "' ](--[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*)[ "' ] """ ) SKIP = { " .venv " , " venv " , " build " , " dist " , " node_modules " } def rec ( kind , name , path , line , text ): digest = hashlib . sha256 ( f " { path } \n { text } " . encode ()). hexdigest ()[: 10 ] return { " id " : f " { kind } : { name } " , " kind " : kind , " name " : name , " path " : path , " line " : line , " text " : text , " digest " : digest } def scan_file ( path ): src = path . read_text ( encoding = " utf-8 " ) rel , out = str ( path ), [] for node in ast . walk ( ast . parse ( src )): if isinstance ( node , ast . FunctionDef ) and not node . name . startswith ( " _ " ): out . append ( rec ( " fn " , node . name , rel , node . lineno , f " def { node . name } ( { ast . unparse ( node . args ) } ) " )) elif isinstance ( node , ast . ClassDef ) and not node . name . startswith ( " _ " ): bases = " , " . join ( ast . unparse ( b ) for b in node . bases ) out . append ( rec ( " class " , node . name , rel , node . lineno , f " class { node . name } ( { bases } ) " if bases else f " class { node . name } " )) for lineno , line in enumerate ( src . splitlines (), 1 ): for key in ENV_RE . findall ( line ): out . append ( rec ( " env " , key , rel , lineno , line . strip ())) for flag in CLI_RE . findall ( line ): out . append ( rec ( " cli " , flag , rel , lineno , line . strip ())) return out def main ( root = " src " , out = " build/evidence.json " ): records , seen = [], {} for path in sorted ( pathlib . Path ( out ) dest . parent . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) dest . write_text ( json . dumps ({ " count " : len ( records ), " records " : records }, indent = 2 )) print ( f " { len ( records ) } evidence records -> { dest } " ) return 0 if __name__ == " __main__ " : sys . exit ( main ( * sys . argv [ 1 : 3 ])) Run it from the repository root and inspect the index before trusting it, because duplicates and dead code both show up there plainly. Each line names the file, the stale claim, and the exact source location that moved: $ python evidence_index.py src build/evidence.json 214 evidence records -> build/evidence.json $ python check_docs.py build/evidence.json docs/config.md docs/config.md:5: stale env:APP_API_KEY -> code changed at src/client.py:42 docs/config.md:6: model line has no evidence citation 2 problem(s) across 1 file(s) Step 4 — Draft With a Free Model and Rebuild on a Free Server The drafting call is the only place a model participates, and it receives the fact sheet rather than the repository. A prompt contract that works with small models is deliberately dull, and it forbids the two failure modes that matter: unsupported sentences and invented specifics. Draft text for the regions between <!-- model:start --> and <!-- model:end --> only. State a fact only if it appears in the fact sheet below. End every factual sentence with exactly one citation of the form [[ev:<id>@<digest>]]. If the fact sheet does not support a sentence, omit the sentence instead of guessing. Never write about support, security, pricing, or dates; those sections are human-owned. MonkeyCode's free model access covers this drafting step, and its free server option can run the nightly evidence_index.py plus check_docs.py pair so drift surfaces without a CI budget. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Both availability claims are the operator's, so confirm the current terms yourself before depending on them for a scheduled job; the workflow is provider-neutral and the scripts run anywhere Python 3.9 or newer exists. The scheduled ordering matters more than the tooling, so keep it fixed and boring. Rebuild the index first, then draft new model regions, then run the checker, and never let the checker run against a stale index. If the drafting step fails, publish nothing and leave the previous regions untouched, since a partially regenerated page is worse than an old one. What the Model May Draft, and What a Human Must Own The table below is a starting policy, not a universal rule; adjust it to your risk surface and record the adjustment in the repository. Doc content Model may draft Required evidence Named owner Function and flag reference Yes, inside model regions fn: , cli: , or env: record No Default values and config keys Yes env: or cli: record No Supported platforms list No None accepted Yes SLA, uptime, support windows No None accepted Yes Security posture, data handling No None accepted Yes Pricing, quotas, deprecation dates No None accepted Yes Migration and upgrade guarantees No None accepted Yes Limitations and Who Should Skip This The signature-level digest catches renames, parameter changes, and flag removals, but it does not catch a changed default buried in a function body. Regex scanning for os.getenv and add_argument misses dynamic access such as os.environ[key] or flags built from a config file, so treat index coverage as partial and stated rather than complete. Duplicate symbol names get suffixed ids, which keeps the build green but can still make a page cite the wrong twin. Prose-heavy documents such as architecture narratives gain little here, because most of their value is judgement that no artifact can anchor. Skip this approach if a machine-readable schema already generates your reference docs, since the digests would duplicate a stronger guarantee. Skip it if your team cannot sustain a nightly rebuild, because a stale index produces confusing failures and erodes trust in the gate. Skip it as well if reviewers treat a red build as noise; a gate that everyone mutes is worse than no gate. title: How to catch caption timing drift in a 29.97 fps video export with Python
author: Anlin
summary: A caption that looks fine at the start of a movie recap can land noticeably early or late near the end. Measure the error at several known frames before shifting individual cues. A constant error suggests a shifted start time. An error that grows with elapsed time suggests a clock or frame-rate conversion problem. Cover: AI-generated schematic showing caption cues moving progressively ahead of the frame clock. The gaps are exaggerated and not to scale. Use the exact frame rate Assume a constant-frame-rate export at 30000/1001 fps. Frame 0 and subtitle time 0 share the same origin. Each expected caption onset is a zero-based frame index on the output timeline. The actual onset comes from the subtitle export in milliseconds. Keep the math exact until reporting the result. At frame 17,982, the expected time is 17982 × 1001 / 30000 , or 599.9994 seconds. Treating the same frame index as 30 fps gives 599.4 seconds. The clocks differ by 599.4 milliseconds after about ten minutes. Check three known onsets This example uses fictional data and runs with Python's standard library. Positive error means the caption starts late. One frame is a simple tolerance for this example. Set your real tolerance based on the cues and delivery requirements of the project. from fractions import Fraction fps = Fraction ( 30_000 , 1_001 ) frame_ms = 1_000 / fps # (name, expected output frame index, actual subtitle start in ms) anchors = [ ( ' opening cue ' , 0 , 0 ), ( ' middle cue ' , 8_991 , 299_700 ), ( ' final cue ' , 17_982 , 599_400 ), ] for name , frame , actual_ms in anchors : expected_ms = frame * frame_ms error_ms = actual_ms - expected_ms result = ' REVIEW ' if abs ( error_ms ) > frame_ms else ' OK ' print ( f ' { name : < 12 } { float ( error_ms ) : + 8.1 f } ms { result } ' ) opening cue +0.0 ms OK middle cue -299.7 ms REVIEW final cue -599.4 ms REVIEW Here the captions start early, and the error grows nearly linearly. The fictional subtitle times were deliberately calculated at 30 fps. In a real export, compare the frame-rate metadata and subtitle timing first. If all three errors instead cluster around the same offset, check whether the video, audio, and subtitle exports started at the same point. Know when to use presentation timestamps The frame formula works for constant frame rate with a shared origin. For variable-frame-rate footage, use each output frame's presentation timestamp and apply the track's time base. B-frames can appear in decode order that differs from presentation order, so compare frames in the order viewers see them. Normalize any nonzero stream start to the subtitle timeline before measuring the difference. After fixing a suspected conversion or offset, export again and check the same anchors. Watch one short excerpt around a story cue to make sure the caption lands when the viewer needs it. AI disclosure: AI generated this article and its example. The Python example was executed to verify the output.

title: Building a 3D WebGL & macOS-Style Interactive Developer Portfolio in React
author: Piyush Yenorkar
summary: Most developer portfolios look identical: a generic hero section, a grid of project cards, and a contact form. When building my own developer space, I wanted to treat it like a full-scale interactive web application rather than a static resume. I wanted visitors to explore, interact with 3D physics, run desktop OS windows, and chat with an autonomous portfolio AI assistant. Here is a breakdown of how I designed and engineered my 3D developer portfolio. ⚡ The Live Experience 🌐 Live Website : piyushyenorkar.vercel.app 💻 Tech Stack : React 19, TypeScript, Three.js, @react-three/fiber, Framer Motion, Tailwind CSS, Groq API (LLaMA 3.3). 🛠️ Key Architectural Features 1. 3D WebGL Robot with Interactive Laser Targeting At the core of the experience is an interactive 3D robot rendered with Three.js and @react-three/fiber : Real-time mouse tracking : The robot's head and limbs dynamically calculate Euler angles based on normalized viewport coordinates. Interactive laser targeting : Clicking on interactive elements triggers an explosive laser beam with jitter physics and glowing particle decay. Asset Optimization : Using Draco-compressed glTF models and deferred texture streaming to ensure sub-second initial load times even on mobile. 2. Desktop OS Window Stacking & Multi-Tasking Dock Inspired by macOS and cyberpunk terminals, the bottom navigation acts as an interactive desktop environment with 5 concurrent apps: Direct Messaging & Anonymous Community Chat Autonomous Portfolio AI Assistant Interactive GitHub & LinkedIn OS Viewers The Engineering Challenge: Real OS Z-Index Layering In traditional modals, clicking one popover closes or conflicts with another. To make it behave like an authentic desktop OS: Windows are portaled directly to document.body to avoid local z-index trapping. Implemented an event-driven bringToFront(windowKey) manager. Touching or clicking any window in the background increments the global z-index counter and transitions it above other windows without unmounting or reloading background states. Draggable with inertia via Framer Motion's useDragControls . 3. Retro Memory Chip Insertion for Blog Articles Instead of standard paginated blog lists, the reader treats articles as physical hardware cartridges: When a user selects an article card, the current memory chip ejects with sound and glowing slot animations. Dynamic bounding box coordinate tracking ( getBoundingClientRect ) maps the exact screen trajectory from the sidebar dock to the central reader mainframe. 4. Embedded Autonomous AI Assistant I integrated a dedicated conversational AI into the OS dock powered by Groq Cloud API and LLaMA 3.3 : Built with client-side key rotation and streaming response fallbacks. Knows my full technical background: Pluto Campus (Play Store app with 1st place product pitch), FlowMind (Axion Hackathon 1st place & HackHazards Top 50), SafeShell, and NHAIFaceID (offline edge facial recognition SDK). Generates interactive follow-up suggestion chips so visitors can click through topics effortlessly. 💡 What I Learned WebGL Performance on Mobile : Mobile GPUs struggle with heavy shadows and post-processing bloom. Implementing adaptive pixel ratios ( dpr={[1, 1.5]} ) and conditionally pausing Three.js render loops when out of view saved over 40% battery and CPU overhead. Layering Architecture : Desktop OS window management inside a modern web app requires strict separation between DOM stacking contexts and portal mounts. title: Two robots.txt Files, One Product: The App Host Has Rules, the API Host Has 1,248 Bytes of Licence and No Directives
author: OnePassApps
summary: I work on OnePassApps, so this is our own infrastructure and every number below was measured on it today with plain HTTPS - no browser, no session, no cookies and no JavaScript. One product, two hostnames, two robots.txt files. The one on the app host is 160 bytes of crawler rules. The one on the API host is 1,248 bytes of commentary that contains not one directive. That difference is the whole story, and neither file is wrong. The app host's file: eight lines, every one of them a directive https://app.onepassapps.com/robots.txt answers 200 with 160 bytes and 8 non-empty lines. All 8 are directives, none is a comment: User-agent: * Allow: / Disallow: /api Disallow: /api/ Disallow: /account Disallow: /sign-in Disallow: /sign-up Sitemap: https://app.onepassapps.com/sitemap.xml One User-agent group for everybody, one Allow: / , 5 Disallow paths and one Sitemap line. That last line is the useful one: it points at https://app.onepassapps.com/sitemap.xml , which answers 200 and carries 56 URLs. The API host's file: 20 lines, and every one of them is a comment https://api.onepassapps.com/robots.txt also answers 200, with 1,248 bytes. This one is the opposite shape. It has 20 non-empty lines and 0 of them are directives . There is no User-agent line, no Allow , no Disallow , no Sitemap and no Content-Signal: line either - nothing a crawler could act on. What the file does have is three named signals, defined in its own comment text: # search: building a search index and providing search results (e.g., returning # ai-input: inputting content into one or more AI models (e.g., retrieval # ai-train: training or fine-tuning AI models. And it closes with a legal footnote, in three comment lines: # ANY RESTRICTIONS EXPRESSED VIA CONTENT SIGNALS ARE EXPRESS RESERVATIONS OF # RIGHTS UNDER ARTICLE 4 OF THE EUROPEAN UNION DIRECTIVE 2019/790 ON COPYRIGHT # AND RELATED RIGHTS IN THE DIGITAL SINGLE MARKET. The notice does not name us either: the string onepassapps appears nowhere in those 1,248 bytes. It is a statement about the three uses, not about this site. So the API host tells a crawler what the three uses mean, in prose, and then tells it nothing at all about this site. The file names no path, so nothing on that host is disallowed by robots.txt - the file grants no permission and withholds none. Neither file advertises an API, and only one of them points at a sitemap The app host's file names its sitemap. The API host serves no sitemap at all: https://api.onepassapps.com/sitemap.xml answers 404 with 124 bytes - the same NOT_FOUND envelope that host returns for any path it does not have. There is no Sitemap: line to find on that host either, because the file has no directive lines at all. Which means the two hosts behave the same way from a crawler's point of view and differently from a reader's: the app host hands you a rulebook and a map, and the API host hands you a notice. The two files are even served under different caching rules app.onepassapps.com api.onepassapps.com Bytes 160 1,248 Non-empty lines 8 20 Directive lines 8 0 Cache-Control public, max-age=14400, must-revalidate private, no-store, max-age=0 ETag yes none The app host's file is cacheable for four hours and carries an ETag. The API host's file is private, no-store, max-age=0 and carries no ETag, so every fetch of it is a fresh request rather than a cached copy. Limits One build, one fetch per URL, 8 November 2026, plain HTTPS from one network, no browser and no JavaScript. Both files are a snapshot of one build. This post describes what the two files contain and what a crawler could read out of them; it makes no claim about how any particular crawler or AI agent behaves, and none about the legal meaning of the text it quotes - that is not my call. If you want to see the apps themselves rather than the files that describe them, the guides page lists all of them, and the home page is where the nine apps live.

title: The Evidence Behind an AI Review Verdict
author: Jeff
summary: Quick answer: The verdict is produced deterministically with no model involved, using the evidence the checks actually collect. Drift or failing evidence fails, a lack of verified evidence is inconclusive because an empty result is not a pass, partial verification stays partial, and only fully verified evidence passes. Every evidence item carries a reproducible command and the raw process output, so you can check the basis for the verdict yourself. The four evidence classes Before the verdict is computed, every finding is sorted into a class that says how it was produced. Class Source Role in the verdict Static Typecheck, lint, build, hallucinated API Fails when the command fails Dynamic Test, coverage, smoke Fails on a real run that breaks Contract Schema, type drift Fails on drift against the spec AI hypothesis Model reasoning only Never counts as verified evidence A model-only claim is always a hypothesis, and it does not pass anything on its own. The model can suggest where to look, but the verdict comes from measured evidence, not from confident language. How the deterministic verdict works The verdict follows fixed rules rather than a judgment call. Fail : drift or failing evidence is present. Inconclusive : there is no verified evidence, because an empty result is not a pass. Partial : only some of the required checks could be verified. Pass : the evidence is fully verified. No model participates in this decision. That matters because it keeps the result stable and explainable: the same evidence produces the same verdict every time, and a missing check can never be talked into a pass by a well-written summary. Reproducible command and raw output Trust comes from being able to repeat the evidence, not from trusting the label. Each evidence item carries two things: A reproducible command that produced the result. The raw process output the command returned. To audit a verdict, run the command and compare your output with the recorded output. If they differ, the context may have changed since the review, so rerun rather than trusting either result. An item with no command and no output is not verified and cannot support a pass. A concrete case makes this tangible. A change can pass lint and typecheck while the project has no test script. Those two static checks are verified, but the dynamic layer is unverified, so the verdict reads partial rather than pass. Adding one runnable test and rerunning moves the dynamic evidence from missing to measured, and the verdict updates only then. The label never moves ahead of the evidence. How missing and partial cases behave Real projects rarely produce a clean all-or-nothing result, and the verdict reflects that honestly. When a project script is missing, run checks report it as unverified rather than passed. A dynamic run that never reaches a branch leaves that branch without evidence, which is not evidence that it works. Partial verification stays partial until the remaining checks run. Only fully verified evidence passes, so a mix of green and unknown never rounds up to a green verdict. This is the same logic that keeps an empty test result inconclusive. Silence is not approval, and the absence of evidence stays visible instead of being promoted to success. Powerduck keeps this pipeline transparent, showing the evidence class, the command, and the raw output behind each finding so the deterministic verdict is something you can audit rather than a black box. Frequently asked questions Does the model decide pass or fail? No. The verdict is deterministic with no LLM involved. The model can produce hypotheses, but the pass or fail comes from the measured evidence. Can an AI hypothesis make a check pass? No. A model-only claim is always a hypothesis and never counts as verified evidence. It needs a real check behind it. What happens when only some checks run? The verdict is partial until the remaining checks are verified, and it does not round up to a pass. The bottom line The verdict is a deterministic computation over real evidence, not an opinion. Failing evidence fails, missing evidence is inconclusive, partial coverage stays partial, and only full verification passes, with every item backed by a command you can rerun and raw output you can inspect. Keeping model-only notes as hypotheses and empty results as inconclusive is what stops the system from dressing up silence as success. Learn more in the AI code review guide .

title: Single Source of Truth for School Exams: Applying a Data Principle to Exam Season
author: OROO Kids
summary: Developers know the rule well: keep one source of truth, and derive everything else from it. Duplicate data drifts. Copies disagree. Manual re-entry introduces bugs. School exam season is a near-perfect real-world case study of what happens when that rule is ignored — and of how much calmer things get when it is followed. The failure modes look familiar Conflicting copies: a printed date sheet, a forwarded photo and an older spreadsheet each show different dates for the same paper. Manual ETL: marks are typed into one file, then copied into another, then retyped into a report card template. Every hop is a chance for error. No validation step: results reach families before anyone checks them, so fixes happen in production. Model the workflow as a pipeline Think of exam season as a small pipeline with clear stages: Schedule — dates, classes/sections, subjects, sessions. Validate for constraints: no class with two papers in one slot, sensible gaps before heavy subjects. Publish schedule — one master record; notifications to teachers and parents are derived from it, not written separately. Capture marks — the subject teacher enters data before a deadline. Verify — a second person reviews. Think of it as a code review before merge. Publish results — only verified data moves on, and report cards are generated from that same record. Retro — a short review of what slowed the team down, logged for next term. Each stage reads from the previous stage's output rather than from a separate copy. That is the whole trick. Why the verification gate matters In software, we gate deploys behind reviews and tests because rollbacks are costly. Published results work the same way: once families have seen a mark, correcting it costs trust and time. A simple rule — no publication without verification — prevents most of that pain. Tooling that encodes the pipeline OROO Campus ( https://oroocampus.com ) is a free school ERP and AI operating system for schools and coaching institutes. It manages exams, marks, verification, publication and report cards through connected workflows, with timetable, attendance, fees, communication and transport in the same platform, on the web and on apps including Android. In other words, it applies the single-source-of-truth idea to school operations. Takeaway Whether you are building systems or running a school office, the principle holds: one source of truth, a validation step before publishing, and outputs derived from verified data rather than retyped. title: Testing Async and SSE Flows as a Scenario
author: Jeff
summary: Quick answer: Test an asynchronous or SSE flow as an ordered scenario: start the long-running job, connect to the event stream, assert on the events as they arrive, and confirm the final completion state instead of polling one fixed response. SSE is modeled with a text/event-stream media type and an item schema describing one event, and the scenario engine can follow the real streaming system. Why a single request does not fit async work A long-running task does not return its result in one immediate response. It starts, emits progress over time, and completes later, often through an event stream. A single request that checks only the initial 202 or 200 cannot tell you whether the job finished or emitted the right events. A scenario follows that lifecycle in order. A first step starts the job and extracts a job or stream reference. A later step connects to the SSE stream. Assertions check the streamed events and the final state. How SSE is modeled Server-sent events are represented with a text/event-stream media type and an OpenAPI 3.2 item schema that describes a single event. That keeps the streaming operation a normal path item rather than forcing it into a plain REST shape, and the protocol is preserved when editing rather than silently converted. Stage What the scenario does Start job Send the request and extract the job or stream reference Open stream Connect to the event endpoint and read events as they arrive Assert events Check event types, order, and payload fields Confirm completion Assert the terminal event or final state is reached Assert across the streamed events Streaming assertions differ from a one-shot check because the evidence arrives as a sequence of events. Assert the start step returns the expected accepted status and reference. Assert the stream opens and begins emitting events. Check the event types and order, since progress usually follows a defined sequence. Assert the payload fields on the events that matter. Confirm the terminal event marks the job complete. Asserting the order and the terminal event matters, because a stream that emits progress but never reaches completion is a real defect even when every intermediate event looks fine. The engine runs the connected requests in the main process with streamed progress and a cancel action, so a hung stream can be stopped. When a 200 hides a problem An SSE or async step can return a healthy status while the event payload carries an error or an unexpected shape, just as a 200 can mask a contract break elsewhere. Assert the event fields against the item schema rather than trusting the connection status alone. If the expected events do not arrive, the result is inconclusive or a failure, not a pass based on silence. Multi-protocol support is a supporting capability here. It lets the scenario follow the real system across SSE and other protocols, but it should not be treated as the headline. Scenarios stay outside the OpenAPI document with no x-scenarios keys and run against real connected requests rather than mocks. Powerduck keeps the streaming steps and event assertions in the ordered run, so you can see the exact event where an async flow breaks. Frequently asked questions How is SSE represented in the spec? With a text/event-stream media type and an item schema describing one event. The operation stays a normal path item and is not converted into REST. Can a single request verify a long-running job? No. It only sees the initial response. A scenario starts the job, follows the event stream, and confirms the terminal state across ordered steps. What if the stream never completes? A missing terminal event is a failure even when intermediate events look correct. Assert completion so an unfinished job is caught. The bottom line Async and SSE work calls for an ordered scenario that starts the job, follows the event stream, asserts on the events, and confirms completion. Model the stream with the event media type and item schema, check event order and the terminal state, and do not let a healthy connection status hide a bad event payload or a job that never finishes. The scenario follows the real streaming system, which is what makes it more trustworthy than polling a single fixed response. Read more in the API scenario testing guide .

title: CRM for Cosmetic Surgery and Hair Transplant Clinics in the Gulf: Where Leads Get Lost, and What the System Actually Needs
author: Mythex
summary: A cosmetic surgery or hair transplant clinic in Dubai, Riyadh or Doha can spend a serious budget on Instagram and Google ads every month and still not know how many of those enquiries became patients. The enquiries arrive fine. They get lost somewhere between the first WhatsApp message and the day of the procedure. This article is about that gap: where exactly the leads fall out, what a CRM for this kind of clinic has to do (it's narrower than most software demos suggest), the options as of November 2026, and how to build a simple lead-tracking app yourself if nothing fits. I work at Mythex, an AI app builder that is one of the options, so weigh that section accordingly. Where the leads actually fall out Talk to the coordinators at a few clinics and the same five leaks come up. 1. The first reply is slow, or comes from the wrong phone. Most enquiries arrive on WhatsApp, often on a coordinator's own phone or a shared Business app on one device. When that coordinator is off, in a consultation, or leaves the clinic, the conversation goes with them. A patient who asked about an FUE price at 11 pm and heard nothing by morning has usually messaged two other clinics. 2. Nobody owns the follow-up. Cosmetic patients rarely book on the first message. They ask for a price, then photos, then think about it for weeks. Without a named owner and a next follow-up date on every enquiry, warm leads go cold quietly, and nobody can say which ones. 3. The consultation doesn't connect back to the ad. The clinic knows Meta sent 400 enquiries last month and the surgeon did 30 consultations, but not which campaign, which procedure or which coordinator turned enquiries into consultations. So the budget gets moved on gut feeling. 4. The quote lives in a PDF on someone's laptop. Procedure, graft count or areas, price, deposit, validity date. When the patient comes back three weeks later asking "is the price still the same?", the coordinator searches through their chats. 5. International patients have their own journey. Hair transplant clinics in particular get patients from abroad: travel dates, hotel, airport pickup, a fixed procedure day and a flight home. A missed detail here costs a procedure slot that's hard to refill. None of these is fixed by more ads, and most aren't fixed by a full clinic EMR either. They are lead-management problems. What a CRM for these clinics needs (and doesn't) Strip it down and a cosmetic or hair transplant clinic needs one shared list of enquiries with: Source and campaign on every enquiry (Instagram, Google, referral, walk-in, and which ad or landing page if you have it). Procedure of interest (rhinoplasty, liposuction, FUE, PRP, and so on) and the patient's language and country. Status that matches your real stages: new, replied, photos received, quote sent, consultation booked, deposit paid, procedure done, follow-up due, lost (with a reason). Owner and next follow-up date , so each coordinator opens the app to a list of today's follow-ups, not a scroll through WhatsApp. The quote attached to the enquiry, with an expiry date. A simple report : enquiries, consultations and procedures by source and by coordinator, per month. Arabic and English , because coordinators and patients switch between them. What it does not need on day one: marketing automation, AI chatbots, a patient mobile app or a full EMR. Those can come later, and an EMR in particular is a separate, regulated system. The data rule you can't skip Before choosing any tool, separate two kinds of data. An enquiry (name, phone, procedure of interest, source, quote) is sales data. Medical records (history, consultation notes, before and after photos, consent forms) are health data. In the UAE, the federal health data law (Federal Law No. 2 of 2019) restricts storing and transferring health data outside the country except in specific cases set by ministerial resolution, and Dubai Healthcare City has its own regime on top. Dubai's health regulator also has strict rules on medical advertising, including bans on exaggerated claims like "guaranteed results" and on filming patients during surgery for ads. Saudi Arabia and Qatar have their own rules. Check with your licensing authority or a lawyer for your exact situation, but the practical rule is simple: keep clinical records in your licensed clinic system, and keep the CRM to enquiries and sales. That also makes the CRM choice much easier. Your options (as of November 2026) Aesthetic practice platforms with a CRM built in. PatientNow, aimed at plastic surgery and med spa practices, describes CRM and lead management alongside scheduling, EMR, photos and payments. Pabau, used by aesthetic and wellness clinics in the UK, US, EU and UAE according to its own site, ties its CRM to booking, consent forms and treatment records. These make sense if you're choosing your whole clinic system anyway. Ask in the demo how WhatsApp enquiries get in, because that is where Gulf clinics live, and check where the data is hosted. WhatsApp-first CRMs. Several Gulf vendors sell an inbox that puts WhatsApp, Instagram and website enquiries in one place, with pipelines on top, sometimes connected to a clinic system. Good for leak number 1. Ask who owns the WhatsApp Business number and the conversation history if you leave. A general sales CRM. HubSpot, Zoho CRM or Pipedrive, set up with your own stages and fields. Cheaper and flexible, but you'll do the setup yourself, and procedure-specific fields, quotes and travel details take work. A small custom app. If your process is specific (a hair transplant clinic with international patients, or a group with three branches and different price lists), a simple app built around your stages can fit better than bending a big system. That used to mean hiring a developer. With AI app builders it can now be a few days of work by the clinic manager. Building a simple enquiry tracker with an AI app builder Here's how this looks in Mythex, which builds a working web app with a database from a description in chat, in Arabic or English. These are the prompts I'd type, one at a time: Build a lead tracker for a cosmetic surgery and hair transplant clinic in Dubai. Each enquiry has: patient name, phone (WhatsApp), country, language, procedure of interest, source (Instagram, Google, referral, walk-in, other), campaign name, owner (coordinator), status, next follow-up date and notes. Arabic and English, with Arabic right-to-left. Add these statuses in order: New, Replied, Photos received, Quote sent, Consultation booked, Deposit paid, Procedure done, Follow-up due, Lost. When an enquiry is marked Lost, require a reason from a list (price, chose another clinic, not a candidate, no reply, other). Add a "My follow-ups today" page that shows each coordinator only their enquiries with a follow-up date today or earlier, oldest first, with a WhatsApp button that opens a chat with the patient's number. Add quotes: each enquiry can have a quote with procedure, details (for example graft count or areas), price in AED, deposit, and a valid-until date. Show a warning on enquiries whose quote has expired. For international patients, add arrival date, departure date, hotel, airport pickup needed (yes/no) and procedure date, and a calendar view of procedure dates for the next 30 days. Add a monthly report: enquiries, consultations booked and procedures done, grouped by source and by coordinator, with the conversion rate from enquiry to procedure. After each prompt you get a live preview to click through, and you change what's wrong by describing it ("the status list should start with Replied for Instagram leads"). When it works, you publish it to a link or your own domain. What the team gets, and the honest limits What you get: a real database behind the app, a shared link the coordinators open on phone or desktop, Arabic and English, and the code if you ever want a developer to take it over. Sign-in for your staff is built by the agent when you ask for it. The limits, plainly: Keep it to enquiries. Mythex doesn't host apps inside the UAE, so don't put medical records, consultation notes or patient photos in it. Use it for the sales pipeline and keep clinical data in your licensed clinic system. It doesn't read WhatsApp for you. The WhatsApp button opens a chat; it doesn't import conversations. Connecting the WhatsApp Business API is possible but is a project of its own. Someone has to own it. A custom app needs a person at the clinic who adds the next field when the process changes. If nobody will, a ready-made product is the better choice. For teams When several coordinators and a manager use the tracker, put it in a shared team workspace instead of one person's account, so it doesn't leave with a staff member. On Mythex that's the Business plan (from $50/month): a shared workspace, roles for your staff, members-only apps that only signed-in colleagues can open, and Google Workspace sign-in if your clinic uses Google. There are examples for clinics on the dermatology clinic page , and plans on the pricing page . How to decide Replacing your whole clinic system anyway? Choose an aesthetic practice platform with a built-in CRM, and make WhatsApp enquiries and data hosting demo requirements. Happy with your clinic system, but enquiries live in WhatsApp? Add a WhatsApp-first inbox or a simple enquiry tracker next to it. Start with owner, status and next follow-up date. Process unusual (international patients, several branches)? A small custom tracker is worth trying for a week. Whichever you pick, measure one number for the next 60 days: the share of enquiries that get a reply within an hour and a named owner. Clinics that fix that usually find the ad budget was working better than they thought.
