title: Your Free Server Is Not Your Laptop: A Parity Probe for Five Assumptions That Break on Deploy
author: Jordan Huang
summary: You push. The build goes green. Then it 502s. Sound familiar? The gap is almost never your business logic. It is the environment you quietly assumed. So here is a myth-busting FAQ about free tiers. Claims developers repeat. Evidence you can collect yourself. A corrected mental model after each one. Two claims are on the table, and only two. MonkeyCode offers free model access, and it has a free server option. Those are operator-supplied availability claims. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Everything else — quotas, hardware, sleep policy, storage lifetime — stays unmeasured until you probe it. I have not run the code below against that server for this article. You are the one collecting numbers. Why "works on my machine" is a measurement problem Your laptop and any remote host are different computers. That is not a bug. It is a fact you forgot to write down. When something breaks on deploy, you are not debugging code. You are debugging unstated assumptions. So stop guessing and start enumerating. Myth 1: "Same app, same environment" The claim: I run the same build, so behavior must match. But env vars differ. Working directories differ. The process supervisor differs. Even the timezone and locale may differ quietly. A 12-factor app reads config from the environment. That does not mean both environments hold the same config. Corrected model: a deployment is a new environment, not a copy of yours. Enumerate the facts you depend on, then assert them at boot. Which env vars are present? Presence matters more than value. What is process.cwd() ? Relative paths resolve against it. Is the directory writable? Many apps assume yes. Myth 2: "If it binds locally, it's reachable" The claim: the port works on my machine, so the host will expose it. Locally you often bind 127.0.0.1 . That is loopback only. A container or VM needs 0.0.0.0 to accept outside traffic. Also many platforms inject PORT . Hardcoding 3000 is a guess dressed as a default. Corrected model: binding is a two-part contract — address and port. Read both from the environment. Verify from outside, not inside. Myth 3: "A restart is a no-op" The claim: restarting just reruns my process, so nothing changes. But in-memory state vanishes. Counters reset. Any local file cache might vanish too, depending on where you wrote it. Write to /tmp ? Maybe ephemeral. Write to cwd ? Maybe not writable at all. Corrected model: assume nothing survives a restart. Then prove which parts do. Persistence is a measurement, not a vibe. Myth 4: "Free model access means free inference capacity" The claim: the endpoint answers, so throughput is a solved problem. Access is not capacity. A reachable endpoint tells you one thing only: it answered once, from one place, at one moment. So measure rather than assume. Latency from your laptop is not latency from the host. Rate behavior under concurrency is unknown until you push. Corrected model: treat free access as an envelope you discover. Send a small burst, record outcomes, and set your own concurrency ceiling below it. Myth 5: "Local latency predicts user latency" The claim: my API call takes 300ms at home, so users see 300ms. Your laptop sits close to your network. The host sits somewhere else, with its own route and its own queue. Add cold start on top. The first request after idle is not the thousandth request in steady state. Corrected model: latency is a property of a path, not of a function. Measure from where the code runs. The artifact: a /probe endpoint and a restart test Here is the smallest thing that converts assumptions into evidence. One file, zero dependencies, Node 18+. // probe.js — run: PORT=3000 node probe.js import { createServer } from " node:http " ; import { writeFileSync , mkdirSync , existsSync , readFileSync } from " node:fs " ; import { tmpdir } from " node:os " ; import { join } from " node:path " ; import { randomUUID } from " node:crypto " ; const bootId = randomUUID (); const startedAt = Date . now (); const markerPath = join ( tmpdir (), " probe-marker.json " ); const target = process . env . PROBE_TARGET ?? "" ; function writable ( dir ) { try { mkdirSync ( dir , { recursive : true }); writeFileSync ( join ( dir , `.probe- ${ bootId } ` ), " ok " ); return true ; } catch { return false ; } } function previousBoot () { if ( ! existsSync ( markerPath )) return null ; try { return JSON . parse ( readFileSync ( markerPath , " utf8 " )); } catch { return null ; } } async function upstream () { if ( ! target ) return { skipped : true }; const t0 = performance . now (); try { const r = await fetch ( target , { method : " HEAD " }); return { status : r . status , ms : Math . round ( performance . now () - t0 ) }; } catch ( e ) { return { error : String ( e ?. message ?? e ), ms : Math . round ( performance . now () - t0 ) }; } } const server = createServer ( async ( req , res ) => { if ( req . url !== " /probe " ) { res . writeHead ( 404 ). end ( " not found " ); return ; } const prev = previousBoot (); writeFileSync ( markerPath , JSON . stringify ({ bootId , startedAt })); const body = { bootId , uptimeSec : Math . round (( Date . now () - startedAt ) / 1000 ), node : process . version , platform : process . platform , env : { PORT : process . env . PORT ?? null , NODE_ENV : process . env . NODE_ENV ?? null }, files : { cwd : process . cwd (), cwdWritable : writable ( process . cwd ()), tmp : tmpdir (), tmpWritable : writable ( tmpdir ()) }, previousBoot : prev , upstream : await upstream () }; res . writeHead ( 200 , { " content-type " : " application/json " }); res . end ( JSON . stringify ( body , null , 2 )); }); server . listen ( Number ( process . env . PORT ?? 3000 ), " 0.0.0.0 " , () => { console . log ( `probe on 0.0.0.0: ${ process . env . PORT ?? 3000 } ` ); }); Note the deliberate choices. It binds 0.0.0.0 . It reports env var presence, never values. It returns no secrets. Run the restart test Now call it twice, with a restart in between. curl -s https://YOUR_HOST/probe | tee probe-1.json # restart the service however your host does it curl -s https://YOUR_HOST/probe | tee probe-2.json diff < ( jq -S . probe-1.json ) < ( jq -S . probe-2.json ) Then read the diff like a diagnostic. bootId changed? Good, the process really restarted. previousBoot is null ? That marker did not survive. Your /tmp is not durable. cwdWritable is false ? Drop file-based caches from that path. upstream.ms is large or errors? Measure from the host, not your desk. Set PROBE_TARGET to your model endpoint URL to include it. A HEAD may return 405 ; that is still a useful reachability signal. Guard this endpoint A probe that leaks paths is a reconnaissance gift. Gate it behind a header or remove it after the test. Never reuse /probe as your production health check. It writes files. Health checks should not. Decision table: what belongs where Once the probe answers, placement stops being a debate. Use this table. Workload Your laptop Free server option Why Public HTTP endpoint No Yes Needs an always-on address Long cron batch No Verify first Restarts kill in-flight work Local file cache Yes Only if writable Probe tells you API key storage Never Env vars Never in the repo Model calls under burst No Measure first Access is not capacity Anything with an SLA No No Free is not a contract Read the last row twice. Free is a starting point, not a promise. Limitations and who should not use this This probe reports facts about one process at one instant. It is not monitoring. It will not catch a host that degrades next Tuesday. It says nothing about model output quality either. That is a separate experiment. Skip this approach if you handle regulated data and cannot expose a diagnostics route. Skip it if you need a durability guarantee in writing. Also skip it if you cannot accept a restart wiping state. Pick a platform with durable storage instead of fighting the free one. The one-line takeaway Stop asking "why did it work locally?" Start asking "what did I never verify?" Write the probe. Run it twice. Let the diff argue for you. If you want a cheap place to point the probe at a model endpoint, MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option are enough to start measuring — and you now know exactly what to measure.

title: Will AI Replace Entry-Level PR Jobs? What Juniors Should Do Now
author: Shilika
summary: AI won't remove entry-level PR jobs, but it is removing many of the tasks those jobs were built around: building media lists, clipping coverage, first-draft releases and monthly report formatting. The junior roles that survive will be smaller in number and different in shape, with less volume work and earlier exposure to judgment, writing and reporter contact. If you're starting out, the useful move is to practise the parts of the job a tool can't do, deliberately and early. I'm writing this for juniors, and for the people who hire and train them. Neither group benefits from panic. Which junior PR tasks is AI actually taking over? Be specific, because "AI is taking jobs" is too vague to act on. Most junior PR roles were a bundle of tasks, and the bundle is coming apart. Task juniors traditionally did What AI does with it now What's left for a person Building media lists from scratch Pulls reporters and recent articles by beat in minutes Judging which reporter genuinely fits this story Coverage clipping and monitoring Tracks mentions and summarises them Spotting the one mention that needs a response First drafts of releases and pitches Produces a clean draft from bullet points Finding the angle, checking facts, making it sound human Monthly reports Formats metrics and coverage lists Explaining what the numbers mean and what to change Researching a reporter's past work Summarises their last 20 articles Reading enough to know what they'd actually care about Repurposing content for social Turns one piece into many formats Choosing which version fits which channel Look at the right-hand column. Every remaining task is a judgment call. That's the new entry-level job. What does that mean for the number of junior roles? Honestly, some agencies will hire fewer juniors, because one person with good tools can cover what used to take two or three. I won't pretend otherwise. If your plan was to spend two years doing nothing but media lists and clipping, that path is narrowing. But two things push the other way. First, every company now produces more content, and someone has to check it, which needs people who understand media. Second, the senior people everyone wants to hire had to start somewhere. An industry that stops training juniors runs out of seniors. The firms that think long term will keep hiring juniors and give them better work earlier. For more on why the senior end of comms is getting more valuable, not less, see my field note on whether AI will replace PR . How did juniors learn the job before, and what's lost? The old system had a hidden benefit. Building a media list by hand taught you who covers what. Clipping coverage every morning taught you which stories ran and why. Drafting twenty pitches that got rewritten taught you what a good one looks like. That's the real risk with AI: not that it takes the tasks, but that it takes the learning that came with them. A junior who has never read a reporter's articles, because a tool summarised them, won't develop the instinct that makes senior people valuable. I learned most of what I know by doing the volume work and paying attention. My advice when I wrote about it in 2023 still stands: my advice to anyone starting out is - just learn by doing & then see yourself slay. Shilika Jain on X, 7 Aug 2023 The doing has changed. The principle hasn't. You have to find a way to do the reps even when a tool could skip them for you. The Weekly Reps Plan for junior PR people This is the practice routine I'd give anyone in their first two years. It replaces the learning the old grunt work used to provide, on purpose. Read five stories a week from one reporter on your beat, fully. Not summaries. Note what they lead with, who they quote and what they never write about. Write one pitch a week without AI, then compare it to an AI draft. Find what yours has that the AI version lacks. Usually it's a specific detail or a reason why now. Fact-check one AI draft line by line. Find the source for every claim. You'll quickly learn where models invent things, which is a skill teams now need. Answer every journalist request you're given within the hour. Speed and reliability are how reporters start to trust a name they don't know. Sit in on one interview or prep call. Ask to listen. Notice how the senior person steers the conversation. Write one short opinion piece a month under your own name. A LinkedIn post, a newsletter, a guest blog. Writing in your own voice is becoming rarer and more valuable. Ask one senior colleague "why did you do it that way" each week. The reasoning is what you can't get from a tool. Point four comes from something I believe about the basics: responding and answering journalists’ query is PR 101! Shilika Jain on X, 25 Oct 2023 It sounds small. In practice, the junior who answers reporters fast and accurately becomes the person reporters email directly. That relationship is something no tool can take from you. Which skills should juniors build first? If I had to rank them for someone starting in 2026: Writing without help. Clear, specific, short. AI makes average writing free, so good writing stands out more. Fact-checking and source discipline. Teams that use AI need someone who catches what it gets wrong. Reporter knowledge on one beat. Know the 20 to 30 people who cover your sector and what they care about. Using AI tools well. Prompting for research and drafts, and knowing when not to trust the output. Sector knowledge. In Web3 and AI, understanding the technology is the price of entry. You can't pitch what you can't explain. That last one is how I started. The work was demanding in a way that taught me a lot: love my job although it’s a mental stretch to learn about complex web3 tech,send 100s of emails,follow up w clients at 2AM in the night,break my head in devising new strategies,feeling blank due to too much information overload Shilika Jain on X, 30 May 2023 AI can lighten the "100s of emails" part now. The "learn about complex tech" part is still yours to do. If you're specifically aiming at Web3, my sibling piece on how to break into Web3 communications covers the job search side. What should managers and agencies do differently? If you hire juniors, the old training model doesn't work anymore. You can't rely on volume work to teach them, because the tools do it. So build the learning in deliberately: Old way juniors learned New way to teach the same thing Building lists by hand Have them audit an AI-built list and explain each cut Drafting endless pitches Have them rewrite AI drafts and defend each change Clipping coverage daily Have them write a weekly "what this coverage means" note Shadowing occasionally Bring them into prep calls and debriefs as standard Formatting reports Have them present one insight from the report to the client This also makes juniors useful faster. Someone who can check AI output, spot a weak claim and explain coverage to a client is worth more than someone who can only produce lists. If you're a founder with a junior marketer and no senior PR person to learn from, pairing them with a fractional operator is one way to get both the work and the training. It's the kind of engagement I offer through AI startup PR . Where is this advice wrong for you? A few honest exceptions: In very small teams or solo setups, there may be no junior role at all. Your path in might be freelancing, content writing or a role adjacent to PR, like community or social, and moving across. In some regions and languages, AI tools are weaker, and native-language media work still relies heavily on people. Juniors with strong regional language skills have an edge there. In highly regulated sectors, the review and compliance side grows, and juniors may spend more time on accuracy checks than on pitching. That's still valuable training. And if you love writing but hate pitching, PR may not be the only home for you. Content and editorial roles are changing too, but they reward the same original writing skill. FAQ Should juniors avoid using AI tools so they learn properly? No. Use them, because every employer will expect you to. Just don't let them replace the reps that build judgment. Draft with AI, but also write some things from scratch, and always read the source material yourself before trusting a summary. Is PR still a good career to start in 2026? For people who like writing, people and fast decisions, yes. The work is moving toward strategy and relationships earlier in a career, which is the more interesting part. It's a weaker choice if what you wanted was predictable, repetitive work. What should I put in a junior PR portfolio now? Show judgment, not volume. Include a pitch you wrote and why you targeted that reporter, an AI draft you corrected with your edits marked, and a short piece of original writing under your name. One placement you helped land, with your role explained honestly, beats ten you can't explain. Will AI replace PR interns before it replaces junior staff? Intern tasks are the most exposed, because they're often pure volume work. Good internship programmes will shift toward observation, writing practice and fact-checking. If an internship offers only list building, ask what else you'll learn before you accept it. Training juniors on an AI-assisted team, or starting out yourself? Book 30 minutes with me. I'm Shilika Jain, a fractional PR lead for Web3 and AI founders. More playbooks at shilikajain.com .

title: Streaming A2A Task Status over SSE
author: Jeff
summary: Quick answer: A2A can stream task progress and status over Server-Sent Events, which the desktop shows in the SSE viewer. The stream lets you watch the task move through states rather than poll blindly, and the final result is read when the task reaches a terminal state. Stopping the local view ends the stream, but it does not cancel the remote work, which still needs a CancelTask request. Why streaming fits a long-running task A task that takes time produces a poor experience when the only option is to wait and poll. The caller has no sense of progress, and a hung run looks identical to a slow one until a timeout decides. SSE changes that by pushing events as the task advances, so the status stays current without repeated requests. The SSE viewer turns those events into a readable timeline of the task. What the stream carries Element What it tells you Status events The task's current state as it changes Progress events How the work is advancing Artifacts Outputs produced before the terminal state Terminal event The task completed, failed, or was cancelled The task moves through defined states, and the events preserve that order rather than collapsing it into a single final answer. Take a task that processes a batch of records. The first event confirms the task started, progress events report the count as each batch completes, and a terminal event carries the summary when the work finishes. Watching the sequence, the caller can see the task advancing rather than guessing, and a stall where the count stops moving is visible long before a timeout. If the caller decides the work is no longer needed halfway through, closing the viewer leaves the batches running on the server, and a CancelTask request is the only step that stops them. The same events that make progress visible also make a hung run easy to spot, which is the practical reason to prefer the stream over a blind wait. How to read the stream honestly Open the SSE viewer after the task is submitted. Read the events in order and note the state transitions. Distinguish progress from a terminal state. Read the final result or artifact when the task completes. Keep the stream separate from the question of cancellation. A stream that stops producing events is not the same as a task that ended. The absence of an event can mean a quiet period or a hung run, and without a terminal event you should check the status rather than assume completion. Set an expected duration so a silent run gets investigated instead of left open. The local and remote boundary The viewer is a client of the stream, and the local Stop action ends what happens on the desktop, the connection and the displayed events. It does not send a cancellation to the remote agent, and the task can keep running and emitting on the server. To stop the work, send a CancelTask request and confirm the status, rather than assuming closing the viewer reached the agent. This is the same boundary that keeps the desktop view from being mistaken for control over the remote process. The stream is a view into the task, not a handle that cancels it. Powerduck keeps the SSE viewer and the separate cancellation path in the desktop, so progress and control stay distinct. Frequently asked questions Does SSE replace polling? It pushes status and progress as events, so you can watch the task without repeated polling, though you still wait for a terminal event. What if the stream goes quiet? Without a terminal event, check the status rather than assuming completion, and set a duration threshold for investigation. Does closing the viewer cancel the task? No. It ends the local stream, and remote work needs a CancelTask request. The bottom line SSE gives you a live, ordered view of an A2A task, streaming status, progress, and artifacts into the viewer until a terminal event arrives. Read the events in order, do not mistake a quiet stream for completion, and keep the viewer separate from cancellation. The local Stop ends the view rather than the remote work, which still needs a CancelTask request. The stream is a window into the task, not a control over it. Continue in the A2A guide .
